virals.name: Anton Gerashchenko
virals.hook:
The Republicans’ electoral defeat weakens Trump at home but leaves him considerable freedom of action in foreign policy. Towards the end of their second terms, American presidents have often focused on international affairs to demonstrate their ability to deliver results: Bill Clinton sought an Israeli–Palestinian peace agreement, Barack Obama concluded the nuclear deal with Iran and restored relations with Cuba, and George W. Bush increased the US military presence in Iraq after the Republicans’ defeat in the 2006 elections. Trump, too, may step up his foreign policy initiatives in pursuit of quick wins.

Trump has already created a degree of turbulence in US foreign policy. Let us hope it does not turn into a nosedive. His scope for quick diplomatic successes is limited: previous negotiations with Putin and Xi Jinping have produced no significant results, while new agreements would require time and mutual concessions. Decisions on limited military operations, however, can be taken much more quickly.

Iran remains an area where both a negotiated end to the war and renewed escalation are possible. The war and the resulting rise in prices were among the reasons for American voters’ discontent. Trump may try to end the conflict through an agreement, presenting it as the result of US military pressure. However, Tehran sees that he has been weakened politically and may be in no hurry to make concessions. In that case, the president may resort to further strikes in the hope of changing Iran’s position.

On Iran, Trump can count on support from some Democrats, though mainly for specific measures. Senator John Fetterman has consistently supported forceful military action, while Congressman Josh Gottheimer backed the initial strikes but argued for limiting the duration of the operation. Democrats may support sanctions, efforts to curb Iran’s nuclear programme or a diplomatic agreement, but they are unlikely to agree to another prolonged war. Congress will be able to tighten scrutiny of military spending, though its ability to block particular presidential decisions will remain limited.

On Russia, Trump may talk about negotiations, but the Kremlin remains unwilling to end the war. Trump may therefore try to secure a limited agreement, such as a ceasefire or a freeze in hostilities, that he can present as a diplomatic success. However, without reliable security guarantees, such a deal would leave Russia able to resume its aggression. Broader agreements with Putin and Xi Jinping, including on strategic stability, also remain difficult because of differences between the parties.

The new Congress will make it harder to implement agreements involving major concessions to Russia. Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons, Richard Blumenthal, Jacky Rosen and Chuck Schumer have previously supported peace initiatives while insisting on security guarantees for Ukraine, respect for its sovereignty and sanctions pressure on Moscow. They may support further sanctions or negotiations for a lasting peace, but they will oppose unilateral concessions to the Kremlin.

In relations with Europe, Trump has more scope for cooperation with Democrats, particularly on defence spending. Many Democrats, including Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons and Dick Durbin, agree that European countries need to contribute more to their own security. However, Trump also sees this as an opportunity to reduce US commitments, whereas most moderate Democrats support maintaining America’s leading role in NATO. At the same time, the view that Europe should take greater responsibility is gaining ground within the Democratic Party. Even a change of president in 2028 would therefore not guarantee a return to the previous model of transatlantic relations. Trump may also continue to use tariffs, threats to reduce the US military presence and other means of putting pressure on allies.

A separate risk is the possibility of a military operation against Cuba. The administration is already imposing severe economic restrictions, and regime change in Cuba remains one of Marco Rubio’s priorities. Trump may see Cuba as a place where he can quickly demonstrate results without complicated negotiations with major powers. However, regime change by force could trigger a humanitarian crisis, a new wave of refugees and growing discontent among Americans.

The electoral defeat is also accelerating the struggle over the future of the Republican Party after Trump. Republican politicians must weigh the fact that his support helps them win primaries, while close ties to an unpopular president can hurt them in general elections. Potential successors, including JD Vance, Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis, represent different visions for the party’s future. Yet an open break with Trump remains risky because of his influence over Republican voters. The struggle for leadership is therefore likely to involve a gradual distancing from particular presidential decisions, especially on the economy, tariffs and Iran.

Following the elections, Trump is weaker at home, but his foreign policy decisions may become less predictable. In the near term, two developments will be worth watching: whether he tries to compensate for diplomatic difficulties through military escalation, and how quickly Republicans begin distancing themselves from his decisions as they prepare for the 2028 elections.

outsiders.name: Anton Gerashchenko
outsiders.hook:
The Republicans’ electoral defeat weakens Trump at home but leaves him considerable freedom of action in foreign policy. Towards the end of their second terms, American presidents have often focused on international affairs to demonstrate their ability to deliver results: Bill Clinton sought an Israeli–Palestinian peace agreement, Barack Obama concluded the nuclear deal with Iran and restored relations with Cuba, and George W. Bush increased the US military presence in Iraq after the Republicans’ defeat in the 2006 elections. Trump, too, may step up his foreign policy initiatives in pursuit of quick wins.

Trump has already created a degree of turbulence in US foreign policy. Let us hope it does not turn into a nosedive. His scope for quick diplomatic successes is limited: previous negotiations with Putin and Xi Jinping have produced no significant results, while new agreements would require time and mutual concessions. Decisions on limited military operations, however, can be taken much more quickly.

Iran remains an area where both a negotiated end to the war and renewed escalation are possible. The war and the resulting rise in prices were among the reasons for American voters’ discontent. Trump may try to end the conflict through an agreement, presenting it as the result of US military pressure. However, Tehran sees that he has been weakened politically and may be in no hurry to make concessions. In that case, the president may resort to further strikes in the hope of changing Iran’s position.

On Iran, Trump can count on support from some Democrats, though mainly for specific measures. Senator John Fetterman has consistently supported forceful military action, while Congressman Josh Gottheimer backed the initial strikes but argued for limiting the duration of the operation. Democrats may support sanctions, efforts to curb Iran’s nuclear programme or a diplomatic agreement, but they are unlikely to agree to another prolonged war. Congress will be able to tighten scrutiny of military spending, though its ability to block particular presidential decisions will remain limited.

On Russia, Trump may talk about negotiations, but the Kremlin remains unwilling to end the war. Trump may therefore try to secure a limited agreement, such as a ceasefire or a freeze in hostilities, that he can present as a diplomatic success. However, without reliable security guarantees, such a deal would leave Russia able to resume its aggression. Broader agreements with Putin and Xi Jinping, including on strategic stability, also remain difficult because of differences between the parties.

The new Congress will make it harder to implement agreements involving major concessions to Russia. Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons, Richard Blumenthal, Jacky Rosen and Chuck Schumer have previously supported peace initiatives while insisting on security guarantees for Ukraine, respect for its sovereignty and sanctions pressure on Moscow. They may support further sanctions or negotiations for a lasting peace, but they will oppose unilateral concessions to the Kremlin.

In relations with Europe, Trump has more scope for cooperation with Democrats, particularly on defence spending. Many Democrats, including Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons and Dick Durbin, agree that European countries need to contribute more to their own security. However, Trump also sees this as an opportunity to reduce US commitments, whereas most moderate Democrats support maintaining America’s leading role in NATO. At the same time, the view that Europe should take greater responsibility is gaining ground within the Democratic Party. Even a change of president in 2028 would therefore not guarantee a return to the previous model of transatlantic relations. Trump may also continue to use tariffs, threats to reduce the US military presence and other means of putting pressure on allies.

A separate risk is the possibility of a military operation against Cuba. The administration is already imposing severe economic restrictions, and regime change in Cuba remains one of Marco Rubio’s priorities. Trump may see Cuba as a place where he can quickly demonstrate results without complicated negotiations with major powers. However, regime change by force could trigger a humanitarian crisis, a new wave of refugees and growing discontent among Americans.

The electoral defeat is also accelerating the struggle over the future of the Republican Party after Trump. Republican politicians must weigh the fact that his support helps them win primaries, while close ties to an unpopular president can hurt them in general elections. Potential successors, including JD Vance, Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis, represent different visions for the party’s future. Yet an open break with Trump remains risky because of his influence over Republican voters. The struggle for leadership is therefore likely to involve a gradual distancing from particular presidential decisions, especially on the economy, tariffs and Iran.

Following the elections, Trump is weaker at home, but his foreign policy decisions may become less predictable. In the near term, two developments will be worth watching: whether he tries to compensate for diplomatic difficulties through military escalation, and how quickly Republicans begin distancing themselves from his decisions as they prepare for the 2028 elections.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
Putin and Russia have repeatedly saved the Islamic Republic from collapse.

Much as they are doing again now, they have historically intervened when the regime and its allies were at their weakest.

The clearest example came in 2015, when Bashar al-Assad’s forces were losing Syria and the Islamic Republic’s intervention was failing to reverse the battlefield.

Assad controlled roughly one-fifth of the country. Rebel advances threatened the Alawite coastal stronghold, Russia’s Mediterranean naval presence and the Islamic Republic’s land corridor to Hezbollah.

The IRGC, Hezbollah and foreign Shia militias had kept Assad alive on the ground, but they lacked the airpower needed to stop his collapse.

Qasem Soleimani travelled to Russia in July 2015 despite a United Nations travel ban. He reportedly met Putin and senior Russian military officials, placed a map of Syria before them and explained how close the regime was to losing its most important Arab ally.

Soleimani offered the arrangement that would transform the war. Russia would provide overwhelming airpower while the Islamic Republic and its proxies supplied the ground forces.

Russia began its air campaign two months later.

The intervention rescued Assad, preserved Russia’s Mediterranean foothold and protected the Islamic Republic’s route to Hezbollah. It also demonstrated a recurring pattern. When the regime’s own military power proved insufficient, Russia supplied the capability needed to prevent a strategic defeat.

Eleven years later, the Islamic Republic is again under severe military, economic and diplomatic pressure, and another senior regime operative has been sent to Putin.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and the Supreme Leader’s representative, met Putin on November 5 and delivered a message from Mojtaba Khamenei.

Rezaei is now setting the regime’s conditions on the Strait of Hormuz, nuclear negotiations and the post-war security order. His meeting with Putin reportedly addressed regional developments, assistance in ending the conflict and practical economic projects, including a proposed Russian gas pipeline intended to relieve the Islamic Republic’s shortages.

The timing matters.

On the same day, reporting based on leaked Russian defence-industry documents indicated that Russia had arranged to supply the Islamic Republic with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for advanced guided missiles used extensively in Ukraine.

The relationship also includes negotiations or agreements involving Su-35 fighter aircraft, Yak-130 trainers, missiles and other military systems. The Islamic Republic previously supplied Russia with large numbers of Shahed drones for its war against Ukraine. Russia is now positioned to repay that assistance with weapons, diplomatic protection and economic support.

This is not an alliance built on loyalty. It is an exchange between two isolated systems that help each other survive pressure from the West.

Russia gains drones, energy opportunities, access to the Persian Gulf and a partner capable of disrupting American interests. The Islamic Republic gains military technology, diplomatic cover and an external power willing to prevent its complete strategic isolation.

The 2015 intervention shows why the current Putin-Rezaei meeting cannot be dismissed as ceremonial. Soleimani once went to Russia when Assad was approaching collapse and returned with the airpower that saved the Islamic Republic’s regional project.

Rezaei has now arrived while the Islamic Republic itself is under pressure.

Russia may not fight the regime’s war for it or provide every weapon it requests. Its support remains transactional and limited by Russian interests. But history shows that Putin does not need to rescue the Islamic Republic completely to change the outcome. He only needs to provide enough weapons, money, energy and diplomatic protection to keep it alive.

Russia saved the Islamic Republic’s most important regional ally in 2015. The question now is how far Putin will go to save the Islamic Republic itself.

outsiders.name: John Spencer
outsiders.hook:
Last day in Baku. Visited the "Free Woman" or "Unveiling" statue.  As a Western visitor to Azerbaijan, there are many surprises. One is the secular nature of a Muslim-majority country where women are not required to cover their hair, can dress as they choose, serve in government, and pursue careers across society. In the middle of Baku stands the Free Woman monument or statue of a liberated woman, depicting a woman removing her veil. Erected in 1960, it symbolizes Azerbaijani women’s emancipation, their freedom to abandon the veil, pursue education, and participate in public life.

That history remains relevant today. Azerbaijan recently tightened school uniform rules, restricting the hijab in public schools in defense of its longstanding secular tradition. Not a nationwide ban on the hijab as some media have claimed, but school dress restriction. Women are free to wear it outside school.

I find the contrast with neighboring Iran striking, especially when it comes to women’s freedoms, including control over their own appearance and lives. 

In Iran, 22-year-old Mahsa Amini died in September 2022 after being arrested by the morality police for allegedly violating hijab rules and then beaten to death in captivity. Her story is one of many of the human rights violation by Islamic Regime in Iran’s against their own society that includes murder, torture, sexual violence, and persecution of women, mowing down protestors with machine guns.

Be more like Azerbaijan.

outsiders.name: Salih Yilmaz
outsiders.hook:
US-Iran conflict latest:

1. Qatar is still trying to bridge the gap -- the Emir spoke with Trump about efforts to support negotiations toward a broader agreement ending the conflict.

2. Iran has reportedly sent Washington a nuclear proposal via Qatar -- Reuters says Tehran wants its demands addressed before substantive discussions move forward, underscoring that major differences remain.

3. Hormuz is part of the diplomatic track too -- Oman and Iran have discussed practical arrangements aimed at resuming navigation through the strait and moving toward more durable understandings.

4. Trump is still weighing the next step -- Axios reports he met with his national security team and said a decision on Iran would come “soon.”

5. Military activity has not stopped -- the Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Najran.

Bottom line: diplomacy looks more active than it did a week ago, but there is still no agreement on Hormuz, sanctions or the broader conflict.

That uncertainty is also showing up in oil: Brent has rebounded back toward $100/bbl after this week’s sharp selloff. #OOTT

outsiders.name: Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib
outsiders.hook:
Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamic Republic of Iran, and an array of anti-Western groups and networks are unsurprisingly celebrating the Democrats’ sweep of the House and Senate. While the wars in Gaza and Iran contributed to yesterday’s Republican wipeout, most Americans are focused on their worsening economic prospects. High energy costs, persistent inflation, job outsourcing, AI anxiety, doubts about the value of university education, and fears of permanent middle-class stagnation drove the results. Some candidates blamed the President and Republicans for corruption, indifference, inequality, and reckless spending; others emphasized aggressive deportations, racism, bigotry, elitism, and deteriorating civil discourse.

For some Democratic candidates, however, anti-Israel politics, Israel and Palestine, and the war with Iran anchored both their campaigns and political identities. They linked affordability to aid to Israel and the Iran war, presenting America’s political crises and voters’ broader troubles as the consequence of pro-Israel lobbying and politics.

The question now is whether these newly elected Democrats intend to actually tackle affordability, or whether it was a Trojan horse to ascend to power and gain relevance. Blaming aid to Israel will do little to lower grocery prices, especially when this aid is likely to end soon and is a negligible line item of overall U.S. expenditure. Many voters care about Gaza, the Middle East, Russia, and Iran, and deeply consider their geopolitical and economic implications, but most prioritize their immediate circumstances over foreign policy.

Yesterday’s winners must be frustrated American voters; not Hamas, the Iranian regime, or the Muslim Brotherhood.
